opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it came out of a kind of frustration. We had spent years at the hospital carefully curating and annotating CT scans, things like liver and pancreatic tumors, and every time we built a model, we'd hit the same wall: we had no idea how it compared to what anyone else was doing. Everybody was working on their own private datasets, with their own ways of measuring success, so you couldn't really tell whether a new method was better or just tuned to one particular collection of images.

And annotated medical data is incredibly expensive to produce. It takes radiologists and clinicians hours to outline structures slice by slice. It felt almost wasteful to have that sitting on a server, used by one small group, when it could be pushing the whole field forward. So the idea was: if we put it out there with clear tasks and a common evaluation, we'd get a lot of smart people from computer science, engineering, and physics working on clinically meaningful problems they might never otherwise have access to.

There was also a bigger question we cared about, which was generalizability. Rather than asking "can you build the best algorithm for this one organ," we wanted to ask "can you build something that works across many different tasks, different anatomy, different imaging types, without being hand-crafted for each one?" That's much closer to what we'd actually need to deploy these tools in a real clinic. A challenge format was the best way to test that honestly, because you can't quietly overfit to data you haven't seen.

And it worked better than we hoped. Seeing the methods that came out of it, and how widely the data has been reused since, made all the effort of de-identifying, organizing, and releasing it feel very worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response says teams worked on private datasets and could not compare methods, then explains that releasing the expensively annotated data would give other researchers access and enable common evaluation.

r002.rationale: It describes CT scans annotated for the hospital’s own modeling work and says releasing that data would let a broader research community use it to advance the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, it came out of frustration more than anything. When I was at Memorial Sloan Kettering, we were sitting on this enormous collection of CT scans of patients with colorectal liver metastases, and our team of radiologists and research staff had spent years carefully segmenting the liver and the tumors by hand. That annotation is incredibly expensive. It takes a trained person maybe an hour or more per case, and you can't just outsource it to anyone, because you need someone who actually knows what a metastasis looks like next to a vessel or a cyst.

So we had this gold-standard data, and we were building our own segmentation models on it, but I kept thinking, we're one lab. We have a handful of people working on this. Meanwhile there's this whole community of medical image computing researchers at MICCAI with brilliant ideas, and most of them can't get access to clinical data at all, because it's locked behind institutional firewalls and privacy agreements. That mismatch felt wasteful. The bottleneck in the field wasn't ideas, it was data.

The other piece was that I wanted an honest comparison. When everyone trains and tests on their own private dataset, you can't tell whether a method is actually better or whether it just had cleaner data. A challenge forces everyone onto the same footing. Same training set, same hidden test set, same metrics, and you find out very quickly what actually works.

And then the clinical motivation underneath all of it is that liver tumor segmentation really matters for patients. Surgeons need to know how much liver they can take out and how much they'll leave behind. Oncologists need to track whether tumors are responding to chemotherapy. Doing that by hand is slow and inconsistent between readers. If opening up the data to a few hundred researchers could get us to reliable automated tools even a couple of years sooner, that seemed like a far better use of all those hours of annotation than keeping it in-house.

So we went through the de-identification process, worked with the IRB, and put it out there. The response was more than I expected, and it also taught me a lot about how much the way you frame a problem shapes what the community builds.

r001.rationale: The response says most researchers cannot access clinical data, then explains that private datasets make comparisons unreliable and a challenge puts everyone on the same footing.

r002.rationale: It explains that the team had spent years annotating scans while building its own segmentation models, then made that annotated dataset available through the challenge.

astra-6.text: We wanted to bring more people into the problem. Annotated clinical data takes a tremendous amount of time and expertise to put together, and researchers often don’t have access to it. By turning it into a challenge, we could give people a shared dataset and a common way to evaluate their methods. That lets us compare approaches, see where they struggle, and hopefully move toward tools that are useful in clinical practice.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers often lack access to annotated clinical data and that the challenge provides a common way to evaluate methods. It does not connect that access problem to a lack of benchmarking.

r002.rationale: The response describes turning annotated clinical data into a challenge, but does not say the annotations were originally produced for other research.

sol-6.1.text: We’d put a tremendous amount of effort into annotating our clinical images, and I wanted that work to benefit more than just our own lab. Turning the data into a challenge gave researchers a shared problem and a common way to compare their methods. It was also a way to bring the clinical and medical image computing communities together—to see what researchers could do with real clinical data and move toward tools that could ultimately help patients.

r001.rationale: The response says the challenge enabled shared comparisons, but does not connect a lack of benchmarking to researchers’ lack of access to well-annotated data.

r002.rationale: It says the annotations could benefit researchers beyond the lab, but does not say they were originally produced for other research.
